title: Do you want to be healed? (John 5:1–9)
hookLine: a man by the pool thirty-eight years; Jesus asks the obvious question
carry: do you want to be well?

lines: A POOL BY THE SHEEP GATE.
FIVE PORCHES, ONCE THOUGHT A SYMBOL.
cards: Jerusalem, near the Sheep Gate. A pool ringed by covered walkways, and under them, sick people lying on mats: blind, lame, withered.

"Now there is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches." For centuries some readers thought the five porches were invented, a symbol.

Then archaeologists dug near the Church of Saint Anne and found two large pools with colonnades: four around the sides and one across the middle. Five. Under one lies a man who has been ill for thirty-eight years.

teach.b: Jesus learns how long he's been there and asks a question that sounds almost rude: "Wilt thou be made whole?" Of course he does. Doesn't he?

"Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me." People believed the first one in when the water stirred would be healed.
Thirty-eight years, and not one friend to carry him the last few feet. His answer is a list of reasons, and underneath it, loneliness. That's why the question isn't rude.

teach.h: A LIFE BUILT AROUND WHAT'S WRONG.
teach.b: After a long time, a life gets built around what's wrong: your days, your friends, your sense of who you are. Being well would change everything, and change is frightening.
Jesus doesn't argue, and he doesn't use the pool.
"Rise, take up thy bed, and walk." "And immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked: and on the same day was the sabbath."

teach.h: DO YOU WANT TO BE WELL?
teach.b: That last phrase is a fuse; it goes off tomorrow. One detail for the curious: some older Bibles, including the King James, have a verse about an angel stirring the water.
The earliest Greek manuscripts don't include it, so many modern Bibles put it in a footnote. Either way, John's story turns on the question, not the pool.

how: Christians often read this story in services of prayer for healing; some churches anoint the sick with oil, and many simply pray for people by name.

o: perfect, never having done anything wrong
healed and well again, in body and in life
one complete piece, with nothing missing

games.q: you've been lying by the pool for thirty-eight years. a stranger asks: do you want to be well? what do you say?
o: I have no one to put me in the water.
games.why: he explains why he can't: "I have no man... to put me into the pool." Jesus heals him anyway, without the pool.

practice: Think of one thing in your life that isn't well, a habit, a hurt, a grudge, and hear the question: do you want to be well?

Don't answer quickly; notice if your first answer is a reason, like the man's, and whether part of you is afraid of what would change. If you pray, bring the honest answer to God; if you don't, hold it gently.

wordCard.voice: Whole. What Jesus asked a man ill for thirty-eight years if he wanted to be, before he answered with reasons and got up and walked.

orig.note: Greek: whole, sound, healthy. Jesus asks, do you want to become whole?

carryVoice: Your line: do you want to be well? It's a real question, and a kind one. See you tomorrow.
